danish.title: Tiende bog (1812) — Kapitel 28
paragraphs: Mange historikere siger, at franskmændene ikke vandt slaget ved Borodino, fordi Napoleon var forkølet. Havde han ikke været det, ville hans ordrer før og under slaget have været endnu mere geniale, Rusland ville have været fortabt, og verden ville have set anderledes ud. For historikere, der mener, at én mand, Peter den Store, skabte Rusland ved sin vilje, og at det var én mands, Napoleons, vilje, der gjorde den franske republik til et kejserrige og førte de franske hære ind i Rusland, kan den forklaring måske lyde både logisk og overbevisende: Rusland bestod som stormagt, fordi Napoleon var slemt forkølet den fireogtyvende august.

Hvis det kom an på Napoleons vilje, om slaget ved Borodino skulle udkæmpes eller ej, og hvis det var hans vilje, der afgjorde, om tropperne stod sådan eller sådan, så kunne en forkølelse, der hæmmede ham i at udøve den vilje, naturligvis have reddet Rusland. Og så ville den kammertjener, der den fireogtyvende forsømte at bringe ham hans vandtætte støvler, have været Ruslands redningsmand. Følger man den tankegang, er slutningen uomtvistelig. Lige så uomtvistelig som den slutning, Voltaire drog for spøg, uden at vide hvad det var, han spøgte med, da han mente at kunne føre Bartholomæusnattens massakre tilbage til Karl den Niendes mavebesvær. Men tror man hverken, at Rusland blev skabt ved én mands, Peter den Førstes, vilje, eller at det franske kejserrige blev skabt og krigen med Rusland indledt ved én mands, Napoleons, vilje, så forekommer denne tankegang både usand, ufornuftig og i strid med al menneskelig erfaring. Spørger man, hvad der fremkalder historiske begivenheder, melder der sig et andet svar: At menneskenes færden er bestemt fra oven, at den afhænger af, hvordan alle de medvirkendes viljer falder sammen, og at den indflydelse, en Napoleon øver på begivenhedernes gang, alene findes i det ydre, i indbildningen.

Ved første øjekast kan det synes mærkeligt at antage, at Bartholomæusnattens massakre ikke skyldtes Karl den Niendes vilje. Han gav jo ordren og troede selv, at det skete som følge af den. Lige så mærkeligt kan det synes, at nedslagtningen af firs tusind mand ved Borodino ikke skyldtes Napoleons vilje. Han gav jo ordre til at begynde slaget og til at føre det og troede, at det skete, fordi han havde befalet det. Hvor mærkeligt det end lyder, kræver menneskets værdighed, at vi antager denne forklaring. Den siger mig, at hver af os er om ikke mere, så i hvert fald lige så meget menneske som den store Napoleon. Og den historiske undersøgelse bekræfter det til fulde.
Ved Borodino skød Napoleon ikke på nogen og dræbte ingen. Alt det blev gjort af soldaterne. Derfor var det ikke ham, der dræbte folk.

De franske soldater drog ud for at dræbe og lade sig dræbe ved Borodino ikke på grund af Napoleons ordrer, men af egen drift. Hele hæren — franske, italienske, tyske, polske og hollandske — sultne, lasede og udmattede af felttoget — følte ved synet af den hær, der spærrede vejen til Moskva, at le vin est tiré et qu'il faut le boire — vinen var skænket og måtte drikkes. Havde Napoleon på det tidspunkt forbudt dem at kæmpe mod russerne, ville de have slået ham ihjel og derefter kæmpet mod russerne alligevel — for det var uundgåeligt.

Da de hørte Napoleons proklamation, som til erstatning for lemlæstelse og død tilbød dem eftertidens ord om, at de havde været med i slaget foran Moskva, råbte de »Vive l'Empereur!« — ligesom de havde råbt »Vive l'Empereur!« ved synet af tegningen med drengen, der gennemborede jordkloden med en stok; ligesom de ville have råbt »Vive l'Empereur!« ved hvad som helst, man havde vist dem. Der var intet andet at gøre end at råbe »Vive l'Empereur!« og drage i kamp for at finde mad og hvile som sejrherrer i Moskva. De gjorde det altså ikke på grund af Napoleons ordrer.

Og det var ikke Napoleon, der ledede slagets gang. Ingen af hans ordrer blev udført, og mens slaget stod på, vidste han ikke, hvad der foregik foran ham. Den måde, de mennesker slog hinanden ihjel på, blev altså ikke afgjort af Napoleons vilje. Det skete uafhængigt af ham, i overensstemmelse med viljen hos de hundredtusinder, der tog del i den fælles handling. Kun for Napoleon så det ud, som om alt skete efter hans vilje. Og så har spørgsmålet om, hvorvidt han var forkølet den dag, lige så lidt historisk interesse som forkølelsen hos den ringeste soldat ved trænet.

Desuden er påstanden fra diverse forfattere om, at hans forkølelse var årsag til, at hans dispositioner ikke var så velplanlagte som ved tidligere lejligheder, og at hans ordrer under slaget ikke var så gode som før, fuldstændig grundløs — hvilket igen viser, at historieskrivernes fortolkning ikke stemmer.

Den slagplan, der er gengivet ovenfor, var på ingen måde ringere end dem, han tidligere havde vundet sejre med. Den var snarere bedre. De såkaldte ordrer, han gav under slaget, var heller ikke værre end før. De var omtrent som de plejede. Hvis planen og ordrerne tager sig dårligere ud end de tidligere, skyldes det alene, at Borodino var det første slag, Napoleon ikke vandt. Selv de mest gennemtænkte planer og de ypperste ordrer tager sig elendige ud, når slaget er tabt, og enhver militærlærd kan med vigtig mine påvise deres fejl. De sletteste planer og ordrer tager sig derimod fortræffelige ud, når slaget er vundet, og alvorlige mænd fylder bind efter bind med beviser på deres fortrin.

De dispositioner, Weyrother udarbejdede til Slaget ved Austerlitz, var et mønster på fuldkommenhed inden for den genre, men alligevel blev de kritiseret — netop kritiseret for deres fuldkommenhed, for deres overdrevne detaljering.

Napoleon udfyldte ved Borodino sin rolle som magtens repræsentant lige så godt som — ja, endda bedre end — ved andre slag. Han foretog sig intet, der skadede slagets forløb; han hældede til de mest fornuftige meninger, skabte ingen forvirring, modsagde ikke sig selv, blev ikke forskrækket og flygtede ikke fra slagmarken, men bevarede med sin store takt og krigserfaring en rolig og værdig holdning og udførte sin rolle med tilsyneladende kommando.

english.title: Book Ten (1812) — Chapter 28
paragraphs: Many historians say that the French did not win the battle of Borodino because Napoleon had a cold, and that if he hadn't had a cold, the orders he gave before and during the battle would have been even more brilliant, and Russia would have been lost and the face of the world changed. To historians who believe that Russia was shaped by the will of one man—Peter the Great—and that France became an empire and French armies marched into Russia by the will of one man—Napoleon—saying that Russia was saved because Napoleon had a bad cold on the twenty-fourth of August may seem logical and convincing.

If it had depended on Napoleon's will whether to fight or not fight the battle of Borodino, and if this or that arrangement had depended on his will, then obviously a cold affecting the exercise of his will might have saved Russia—and consequently, the valet who forgot to bring Napoleon his waterproof boots on the twenty-fourth would have been the savior of Russia. Along that line of reasoning, such a conclusion is indisputable, as indisputable as the conclusion Voltaire jokingly drew (not knowing what he was joking about) when he said that the Massacre of Saint Bartholomew was caused by Charles IX's upset stomach. But to people who do not accept that Russia was formed by the will of one man, Peter I, or that the French Empire was created and the war with Russia begun by the will of one man, Napoleon, that argument seems not merely untrue and irrational but contrary to all human reality. To the question of what causes historic events, a different answer presents itself: the course of human events is predetermined from above—it depends on the combined wills of all who take part in those events, and a Napoleon's influence on their course is purely superficial and illusory.

Strange as it may seem at first glance to suppose that the Massacre of Saint Bartholomew was not caused by Charles IX's will, though he gave the order and thought it was done because of his order; and strange as it may seem to suppose that the slaughter of eighty thousand men at Borodino was not due to Napoleon's will, though he commanded the battle's commencement and conduct and thought it happened because he ordered it; strange as these assumptions appear, human dignity—which tells me that each of us is, if not more, at least not less of a man than the great Napoleon—demands that we accept this answer, and historical investigation abundantly confirms it.
At the battle of Borodino, Napoleon shot at no one and killed no one. That was all done by the soldiers. Therefore it was not he who killed people.

The French soldiers went to kill and be killed at Borodino not because of Napoleon's orders but by their own volition. The whole army—French, Italian, German, Polish, and Dutch—hungry, ragged, and weary of the campaign, felt at the sight of an army blocking their road to Moscow that the wine was drawn and must be drunk. Had Napoleon then forbidden them to fight the Russians, they would have killed him and gone on to fight the Russians, because it was inevitable.

When they heard Napoleon's proclamation offering them, as compensation for mutilation and death, the words of posterity about their having been in the battle before Moscow, they cried "Long live the Emperor!"—just as they had cried "Long live the Emperor!" at the sight of the portrait of the boy poking the globe with a toy stick, and just as they would have cried "Long live the Emperor!" at any nonsense that might be told them. There was nothing left for them to do but cry "Long live the Emperor!" and go fight, in order to win food and rest as conquerors in Moscow. So it was not because of Napoleon's orders that they killed their fellow men.

And it was not Napoleon who directed the course of the battle, for none of his orders were carried out and during the battle he did not know what was happening in front of him. So the way these people slaughtered one another was not decided by Napoleon's will but happened independently of him, according to the combined will of the hundreds of thousands of people who took part in the common action. It only seemed to Napoleon that it all occurred by his will. And so the question whether he had or hadn't a cold has no more historical importance than the cold of the lowliest transport soldier.

Moreover, the claim by various writers that his cold was the reason his battle plans were not as skillful as on previous occasions and his orders during the battle were not as good as before is quite groundless—which again shows that Napoleon's cold on the twenty-sixth of August was insignificant.

The battle plans cited above are not at all worse but are actually better than previous plans by which he had won victories. His orders during the battle were also no worse than before—they were much the same as always. These plans and orders only seem inferior because the battle of Borodino was the first Napoleon did not win. The most profound and excellent plans and orders seem very bad, and every armchair strategist criticizes them with an air of importance, when they relate to a battle that was lost; and the very worst plans and orders seem brilliant, and serious people fill entire volumes proving their merits, when they relate to a battle that was won.
The battle plan drawn up by Weyrother for the battle of Austerlitz was a model of perfection—yet it too was criticized, precisely for its perfection, for its excessive detail.

Napoleon at the battle of Borodino fulfilled his role as the figurehead of authority as well as—and even better than—at other battles. He did nothing harmful to the battle's progress; he deferred to the most reasonable opinions; he caused no confusion, did not contradict himself, did not panic or run from the battlefield, but with his great tact and military experience calmly and with dignity played his part of appearing to command.
